awd_titl_txt: Conference: Biomedical Engineering/Bioengineering Scholarship in Practice Apprenticeship Workshop
awd_abstract_narration:
Biomedical engineers and bioengineers (BME) address today’s most pressing healthcare challenges by applying engineering principles to biological science. Graduates go on to work in a variety of healthcare fields, including medical devices, therapeutics and diagnostics, and clinical practice. BME faculty are subject matter experts in the science and engineering of biology but are often not formally trained in the science of learning and education research. The purpose of this project is to train a cohort of 15 BME faculty in education research tools that they can use to better support the education and professional formation of future biomedical engineers and bioengineers, a specific goal of the NSF’s Research in Formation of Engineers (RFE) Program.  With this expertise, we will build a community of reflective BME educators who possess the training to evaluate and assess their educational approaches.  

This project will enable a BME Education Research workshop that will broaden and deepen education research participation in the community. The workshop is specifically designed to give participants the space to cultivate their education research ideas in a scaffolded environment with resources to advance their work in real time. Two of the biggest barriers to engaging discipline-based faculty in education research is time and access to the appropriate educational research tools. For this workshop, participants will be mentored by education researchers and implement what they learn. The goal is for participants to use the time and support to develop research plans that can be put into action after the workshop. We will focus on fundamental topics–such as research question development, quantitative and qualitative data collection procedures, and data analysis approaches that are critical for conducting educational research.  The goal is to facilitate active engagement with education research content and utilize a peer-learning environment to develop education research projects. To achieve this goal, the following structure will be implemented: 1. Participant cohorts will be based on shared commonalities in research agenda as defined by a pre-survey; 2. Cohorts will work closely with the mentor team in small groups; 3. Cohorts will also come together throughout the workshop to discuss the fundamental engineering education concepts being introduced. This workshop is designed to prototype an effective multi-day, experiential engineering education research workshop.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Biomedical engineering/bioengineering (BME/BIOE) needs a strong and robust discipline-based education research (DBER) community. Biomedical engineers and bioengineers address today's most pressing healthcare challenges by applying engineering principles to biological science. Graduates go on to play prominent roles across disciplines, from direct clinical healthcare to medical devices, therapeutics, and diagnostics. BME/BIOE is also the most formal interdisciplinary engineering education program today and is commonly, although not entirely, located in research intensive universities (R1). BME/BIOE departmental faculty, responsible for cultivating our future biomedical/bioengineers, typically hail from multiple STEM disciplines themselves and were themselves trained in R1 universities, with minimal exposure to formal pedagogical evidence-based practices and/or education research.

To address this need, the first 2026 Engineering Education Research (EER) Lab for BME/BE Faculty was offered at Northeastern University’s Roux Institute (Portland, Maine) in May 2026.  For the workshop, 25 faculty representing 22 institutions convened to participate in an interactive, experiential workshop designed to accelerate biomedical engineering and bioengineering faculty participation in discipline-based education research (DBER). The workshop addressed the critical need in the BME/BIOE community: while faculty are skilled in technical research and evidence-based teaching practices, many lack formal training in educational research methods.

The workshop followed an active learning model where brief instructional sessions were followed by extended working sessions where participants applied concepts to their own research questions with support from a teaching team and peer feedback. By the end of the workshop, participants developed an outline for an actionable research plan including refined research questions, appropriate theoretical frameworks, research design, data collection strategies, and next steps for IRB submission and publication.

Evaluation results indicate that the workshop achieved measurable positive movement in faculty confidence in understanding EER methods, research question development, knowledge of theoretical and conceptual frameworks, and intent to publish and disseminate.  100% of participants expressed intent to pursue IRB submission and data collection within 12 months, representing a strong behavioral indicator of sustained engagement beyond the workshop.  This workshop was critical to seeding the development of a discipline-based education research (DBER) community in Biomedical engineering/bioengineering (BME/BIOE) that will inform evidence-based pedagogical practices that prepare BME/BIOE students for their interdisciplinary careers.
